stories.title_en: Planting Fake Ingots to Swindle a Village Farmer

paragraphs.zh: 昔有一人，本农家者流也。辛苦耕田，服食淡薄，而性甚悭吝，家颇充裕。外地有骗棍到此地方，知这乡农性贪识惘，遂探其某日当在某处耕田，预将假元宝二个重一百两，埋藏其处。俟乡农正在力耕之时，贼棍故意在其山畔，作左寻右寻状。乡农问曰：“你这人在此寻甚么？”棍云：“我在此寻些东西，你问我则甚？”乡农只得默然。棍又认此树，复认彼树，如有所失状。乡农又曰：“你这人好笑，只管满山认树何为？”棍曰：“实不相瞒，我先父往岁曾被流贼所劫，亦同入伙。后来银子甚多，孤身难带，将银埋在各处，留下一帐登记，欲再来取，不幸死矣。今我依帐来寻此处树下的，不知哪个树是。幸遇你在此，可来助我寻。若寻得，分些与你不妨。”乡农遂带锄同寻。果在一树下，寻得元宝二个。棍佯作喜甚之态，说：“此若寻得，则他处皆可寻了。我实肯分些与你，只是此处无槌凿。”又曰：“此银我无贮藏所在，不如去你家下，代我寻完，分数个元宝谢你，尊意如何？”乡农云：“甚好。”但我与你素不相识，一旦至家下来往，岂不招人疑猜？”棍云：“当诈称是何亲故方好。”乡农云：“有了。我有一妻舅，六七岁时曾卖外江客人，至今并无下落。只认作我妻舅，回来看取姊姊、姊夫，有何不可？”遂将妻父、妻母姓名形状，一一对棍说讫。
paragraphs.en: There was once a man of the farming class. He worked the fields hard, ate and dressed poorly, and was extremely stingy, yet his household was fairly well off. Swindlers from elsewhere came to the place, learned that this farmer was greedy and slow-witted, found out on which day he would be working a certain plot, and in advance buried two fake yuanbao ingots, a hundred taels in weight, at that spot. While the farmer was putting his strength into the plow, the swindler deliberately walked the hillside, pretending to search left and right. The farmer asked, “What are you looking for here?” The swindler said, “I am looking for something. Why do you ask?” The farmer fell silent. The swindler then studied this tree, then that tree, as if he had lost something. The farmer said again, “You are a funny fellow—why keep matching trees all over the hill?” The swindler said, “I will not hide it. Years ago my late father was seized by wandering bandits and even joined their band. Later he had so much silver he could not carry it alone, so he buried it in various places and left a register. He meant to come back for it, but unfortunately he died. Now I am following the register to look under a tree here, and I do not know which tree it is. Luckily I have met you. Help me look. If we find it, I will share some with you; that is no trouble.” The farmer took a hoe and went with him. Sure enough, under one tree they found two yuanbao. The swindler put on a look of great joy and said, “If we found this, the other places can all be found. I truly am willing to share some with you, only there is no hammer and chisel here.” He added, “I have nowhere to store this silver. Better go to your house. Help me finish the search, and I will thank you with several ingots. How does that sit with you?” The farmer said, “Very good. But you and I are strangers. If you suddenly come and go at my house, will people not grow suspicious?” The swindler said, “Then what relative should we pretend I am?” The farmer said, “I have it. I had a wife’s younger brother who, at six or seven, was sold to a traveler from the outer Yangzi; to this day there has been no word of him. Just take yourself for my wife’s brother, come back to see his sister and brother-in-law. Why not?” He then told the swindler one by one the names and looks of his wife’s father and mother.

paragraphs.zh: 遂领至家下，叫妻子出来见舅。其妻相见，问：“弟弟面貌，如何与我不相类？”棍应云：“弟出外省，那边风水不同，以此不类。”其妻又问云：“我父何名，形状何如？母何名，形状何如？”其棍对言不差。又问：“我叔何名，形状何如？”棍应曰：“我小时出去，只记得父母，记不得叔了。”妻遂信之。杀鸡烹鲜，设为盛馔，以待其弟。乡农兄弟诸人，各设席相待甚厚。棍对姊夫曰：“我要些零碎银用，可在你家取过十五六两，与我杂用。”乡农遂取己真银十餘两，与棍用。
paragraphs.en: He led him home and called his wife out to meet her “younger brother.” When they met she asked, “Why does my younger brother’s face not resemble mine?” The swindler said, “I went out to another province; the local air and water are different, so I do not look like you.” She asked again, “What was my father’s name, and what did he look like? What was my mother’s name, and what did she look like?” The swindler answered without a slip. She asked, “What was my uncle’s name, and what did he look like?” He said, “I left as a child. I remember only my parents, not my uncle.” The wife believed him. She killed a chicken, cooked fresh food, and set a rich meal for her “brother.” The farmer’s brothers and the rest of the family each laid feasts and treated him very well. The swindler said to his “brother-in-law,” “I need some small silver for expenses. Let me take fifteen or sixteen taels from your house for mixed use.” The farmer then took more than ten taels of his own genuine silver and gave it to the swindler.

paragraphs.zh: 过数日，棍将帐与姊夫查，更有元宝十餘个，在某山某庵中。其庵无人居住，姊夫带饮食二盒，挑至庵中。时庵中棍已预令二贼在彼伺候，即将乡农背缚于柱中。其二贼抽出牛尾尖刀，再三要杀之。棍佯劝云：“我受姊夫厚款，吃得他兄弟鸡鱼多，勿杀我姊夫。”三贼将饮食吃了即去。其乡农叫天不应，入地无门。至次日午后，一牧童至，乡农叫救命，得解缚归家。妻子问曰：“何待今日方归？舅何不回？”乡农应曰：“勿说他，勿说他。”至今被人骗者，俗语曰“勿说他”。
paragraphs.en: After a few days the swindler checked the register with his brother-in-law: there were still a dozen or more yuanbao in a certain hermitage on a certain hill. The hermitage was uninhabited. The brother-in-law carried two boxes of food and went there. Two other thieves, whom the swindler had already stationed in the hermitage, were waiting. They tied the farmer’s arms behind him to a pillar. The two drew ox-tail daggers and again and again made as if to kill him. The swindler pretended to plead: “I have been treated richly by my brother-in-law and have eaten many of his family’s chickens and fish. Do not kill my sister’s husband.” The three thieves ate the food and left. The farmer called to heaven and got no answer, called to earth and found no door. The next day, in the afternoon, a herdboy came by. The farmer shouted for help and was untied and went home. His wife asked, “Why only come back today? Why did my brother not return?” The farmer said, “Don’t speak of him, don’t speak of him.” To this day, when people have been swindled, the saying is “don’t speak of him.”

paragraphs.zh: 近有江源地方一人，被一棍亦如此骗。其妻有智，即以其元宝凿来与他，知是锡。遂将此棍捆打，勒其供状，始释之。苟非其妻有识，亦蹈前乡农覆辙也。彼时悔之，宁不晚乎！
paragraphs.en: Recently a man in Jiangyuan was swindled in the same way. His wife had wits. She had the yuanbao chiseled and given to her, and knew it was tin. They then bound and beat the swindler, forced a written confession from him, and only then let him go. If his wife had not had sense, he too would have followed this farmer’s ruts. To regret it then—would that not have been too late?

paragraphs.zh: 按：此乡农心苦力勤，啬用薄奉以致富，幸矣！何乃为贪心所使，落贼牢笼，以致失财被辱，反不如江源之妇之智哉！然末世滋伪，奸宄百出，近有丢包贼骗人甚多。更江淮间，又有扯遂法，尤难防检。贼止问你一句，你若答应一句，即被他迷。此妖术也，害人尤多。世道人心，一变至此极乎！偶因前事，遂备述之，以为出途者警。
paragraphs.en: Note: This farmer toiled in mind and body, spent little and lived thin, and so grew rich—fortunate enough! Why let greed drive him into the thieves’ cage, so that he lost money and was humiliated, and fell short even of the Jiangyuan woman’s wits? Yet in these latter days deceit multiplies and villains come in a hundred shapes. Lately the “drop-the-bundle” thieves have taken in a great many people. And between the Yangzi and the Huai there is also the “pull-along” method, still harder to guard against. The thief asks you only one sentence; if you answer even one sentence, you are bewitched. This is demonic art, and it harms still more people. Have the world’s ways and men’s hearts changed to this extreme? I set it down because of the foregoing, as a warning to those who go on the road.

stories.title_en: Taking Bleached Fake Silver at the Maozhou Fair

paragraphs.zh: 钱天广，福建安海人也。时买机布，往山东冒州药王会卖。会期四月十五日起，二十五日止。天下货物，咸在斯处交卸。无牙折中，贸易二家自处。
paragraphs.en: Qian Tianguang was a man of Anhai in Fujian. At the time he bought loom cloth and went to sell it at the Medicine King Fair in Maozhou, Shandong. The fair ran from the fifteenth of the fourth month to the twenty-fifth. Goods from all under heaven were delivered and sold there. There were no brokers to mediate; the two sides dealt on their own.

paragraphs.zh: 一棍以漂白银来买布。每五两一锭，内以真银，如假银一般，色同一样。棍将丝银先对。广以铁槌凿打，并无异样。打至十餘锭，通是一色。广说：“不须再凿槌打。”棍遂以漂白出对，共银六百餘两，内只有细丝银一百餘两，餘者皆假也。银交完讫，布搬去了。广收其银，检束行李，与乡里即雇骡车，直到临清，去买回头货物。取出其银，皆假银也。那时虽悔不及，然广不甚动情，只说云“是我方承得此会，他人出外贸易，从此止矣。”人慨斯人量大，有此大跌，后必有大发也。棍虽脱骗得金数百，然天理昭昭，子孙必不昌隆。盖假银天下处处有之，故录此以为后人之提防，勿蹈天广之覆辙也。按：棍之用假银，此为商者最难提防，必得其梗概，方能辨认。余于壬子秋，在书坊检得一小本仔，辨说银之真假，甚是明白。故录之，以为江湖诸君览之，则假银若一入眼，灼然明白。略陈其一二于左：
paragraphs.en: A swindler came to buy cloth with “bleached” silver. Each ingot was five taels; inside it was genuine silver, made to look like the fake, the color all one. The swindler first matched with silk-thread silver. Guang took an iron hammer and chisel and struck: nothing looked wrong. He struck more than ten ingots; all were the same color. Guang said, “No need to chisel and hammer any more.” The swindler then brought out the bleached silver to match: more than six hundred taels in all, of which only a little over a hundred taels was fine silk-thread silver; the rest was all fake. The silver was paid, the cloth was carried off. Guang put away the silver, packed his bags, and with his townsmen hired a mule cart straight to Linqing to buy goods for the return trip. He took out the silver: all fake. By then regret was too late, but Guang did not take it much to heart. He only said, “It is my luck to have been able to attend this fair; as for other men going out to trade, from now on they should stop.” People sighed that he had a large mind; after such a fall he would surely rise far later. The swindler had cheated several hundred in gold, but Heaven’s principle is clear: his descendants will not prosper. Fake silver is found everywhere under heaven, so I record this as a warning for those who come after, not to follow Qian Tianguang’s ruts. Note: A swindler’s use of fake silver is what merchants find hardest to guard against; you must have the general picture before you can tell it. In the autumn of the renzi year I found a little booklet in a bookshop that explained true and fake silver very clearly. I copy it here for gentlemen of the rivers and lakes to read, so that once fake silver meets the eye it is obvious. I set out a little of it below:

paragraphs.zh: 夫元宝者，坑淘出而原宝。今之官解钱粮，亦倾煎如坑淘出厚色，而成元宝也。俗云“圆宝”是也。
paragraphs.en: Yuanbao: the “original treasure” washed from the pits. Today official shipments of tax silver are also melted and refined to the thick color of pit-washed silver and made into yuanbao. Commonly called “round treasure.”

paragraphs.zh: 松纹，与细丝一样，其皆足色也。
paragraphs.en: Pine-grain (songwen) is the same as fine-thread (xisi); both are full-color, pure silver.

paragraphs.zh: 摇丝，色未甚足。银泻入，以手摇动而成丝也，曰摇丝。
paragraphs.en: Shaken-thread (yaosi): the color is not yet quite full. When the silver is poured in, it is shaken by hand to form threads; hence “shaken-thread.”

paragraphs.zh: 水丝，又名曰干丝，自七成、八成、九成、九五止，通名曰水丝。
paragraphs.en: Water-thread (shuisi), also called dry-thread (gansi): from seven-tenths, eight-tenths, nine-tenths, up to nine-and-a-half tenths, all are called water-thread.

paragraphs.zh: 画丝，即水丝。泻出而无丝，以铁锥画丝于其上，曰画丝。
paragraphs.en: Drawn-thread (huasi) is water-thread. It is poured with no thread; an iron awl is used to draw threads on the surface; hence “drawn-thread.”

paragraphs.zh: 吹丝，即九程水丝。银一入，口含吹筒即吹之以成丝也，曰吹丝。
paragraphs.en: Blown-thread (chuisi) is nine-tenths water-thread. As soon as the silver goes in, a blowpipe is held in the mouth and it is blown to form threads; hence “blown-thread.”

paragraphs.zh: 吸丝，以湿纸盖其上，中取一孔，以银从孔泻下，吸以成其丝也，曰吸丝。今人以铁箔盖于上，亦中取一孔，银从孔泻下，亦吸以成丝也。盖吸丝自七成起，九五止。九五者，亦看得足色也。
paragraphs.en: Sucked-thread (xisi): wet paper is laid over the top, a hole is made in the middle, silver is poured through the hole, and it is sucked into threads; hence “sucked-thread.” Today people use an iron foil on top, likewise with a hole in the middle; silver poured through is also sucked into threads. Sucked-thread runs from seven-tenths up to nine-and-a-half. The nine-and-a-half can also pass for full color.

paragraphs.zh: 茶花，以纹银九钱，入铅一钱，入炉中锅内不用一毫之硝，明倾取出，以把淡底填于脚。后泻银于内，铅方不露，而自成其粗丝也，曰茶花。
paragraphs.en: Tea-flower (chahua): take nine qian of fine silver and one qian of lead, put them in the furnace pan with not a scrap of niter, pour it out openly, pack a pale base into the “feet,” then pour the silver in so the lead does not show, and coarse threads form of themselves; hence “tea-flower.”

paragraphs.zh: 鼎银，即汞银也，又曰水银。以纹银五钱，以汞五钱半，入铁鼎中，倾其色通红于内，取出候冷，拿出其银，止有一两，拆汞五分，可打之而成，或造之以成饼。以银薄贴于外，以墨微洒之，以掩其太白。更能造酒器，及诸项首饰。能拔银丝，亦犹细丝者，只是色略青些。更有赤脚汞银，文银三钱，铜丝二钱，汞五钱半，如同前，倾煎取出，不能打造，亦如同水丝一般。若辨汞银，其色脚嫩，上面银薄贴，色不同赤脚者。然色赤而带嫩，终不如水丝色老。此上古所传。造此换人，亦发家数千。子孙继迹不肖，而家即萧条。害众成家，终不悠久。
paragraphs.en: Tripod silver (dingyin) is mercury silver, also called quicksilver. Take five qian of fine silver and five and a half qian of mercury, put them in an iron tripod, pour until the color inside is all red, take it out, let it cool, and remove the silver: you get only one tael, losing five fen of mercury. It can be beaten into shape or made into cakes. Silver leaf is pasted on the outside and a little ink is sprinkled to hide the too-white color. It can also be made into wine vessels and all kinds of ornaments. It can be drawn into silver wire, still like fine-thread, only a little greener in color. There is also “bare-foot” mercury silver: three qian of fine silver, two qian of copper wire, five and a half qian of mercury; treated as above, poured and refined and taken out. It cannot be worked, and is like water-thread. To tell mercury silver: the color of the feet is tender; the silver leaf pasted on top does not match the color of the bare-foot kind. The color is red yet tender, and in the end not as aged as water-thread. This is what was handed down from ancient times. Those who made it to swap on people also built up thousands for their houses. When descendants followed the trade and were no good, the house at once fell thin. Harming the many to build a house does not last.

paragraphs.zh: 铜，以铜嵌四旁，而后以银泻下，藏其铜于中，曰铜。辨之虽看其丝，终不如细丝之明。其丝粗而带滞碍，即可疑而凿之，方露其铜。
paragraphs.en: Copper (tong): copper is set in on four sides, then silver is poured down, hiding the copper in the middle; this is called “copper.” Even if you look at the threads, they are never as clear as fine-thread. The threads are coarse and catch; that is enough to raise suspicion, and when you chisel, the copper shows.

paragraphs.zh: 铁碎，以铁碎先放于内，然后以银泻诸，适均入其银内，包藏铁于其中。至低者亦有九成，九五者有丝。
paragraphs.en: Iron-bits (tiesui): broken iron is first placed inside, then silver is poured so that it is evenly taken into the silver, wrapping the iron in the middle. The lowest still has nine-tenths; the nine-and-a-half has threads.

paragraphs.zh: 或以铜碎如前，名曰包销银。至低者亦有九成；九五有丝，九成无丝。
paragraphs.en: Or copper bits are used in the same way; this is called wrapped-solder silver (baoxiao). The lowest still has nine-tenths. Nine-and-a-half has threads; nine-tenths has none.

paragraphs.zh: 钞仔铜，用铜一两，入银三分，入炉中。以白信石如硝抽入，泻入中。取出铗四旁者三四分重片，中心者又入炉中倾。再铗，如此者数次。然后用银末，以碗极细，用酸砒草捣汁，入硼砂三分，以罐仔同煮。后放前银末三分，入砒草汁内。以前铜入罐中，以筋炒之，取出，以白水洗去其砒草汁，其色甚白。有一人问曰：“铜中只用银三分，后又以银末三分，何能使银相交于外？”其人对曰：“世间宝物，惟金银为至宝。若先不以银三分入铜倾煎，则后用银末亦为煎煮，必不能入。先以银三分入内，则后用此银末煮之，自然相应也。”故造假银，俗曰“神仙”。然辨此铜，当认银色，乃死鱼白，无青白之色。再看其脚，有两样：或用胭脂点，或用石点。须在点脚及死鱼白处辨之处，则真、赝了然。
paragraphs.en: Chaozai copper: take one tael of copper and three fen of silver into the furnace. White arsenolite, used like niter, is drawn in and poured into the middle. Take it out and clip from the four sides pieces of three or four fen; the center goes back into the furnace to be poured again. Clip again, several times like this. Then take silver powder, grind it extremely fine in a bowl, pound sour-arsenic grass for juice, add three fen of borax, and boil together in a small jar. After that put in the former three fen of silver powder in the grass juice. Put the copper into the jar, stir with chopsticks, take it out, and wash off the grass juice with clear water: the color is very white. Someone asked, “You use only three fen of silver in the copper, then another three fen of silver powder—how can the silver join on the outside?” The answer: “Of the world’s treasures, only gold and silver are the supreme treasures. If you do not first put three fen of silver into the copper and melt it, then later when you boil with silver powder it still will not go in. First put three fen of silver inside, then boil with this silver powder, and they answer each other of themselves.” So making fake silver is commonly called “the immortals’ art.” To tell this copper, look at the silver color: it is dead-fish white, with no blue-white. Look again at the feet: there are two kinds—either spotted with rouge, or spotted with mineral pigment. You must tell it at the spotted feet and the dead-fish white; then true and false are obvious.

paragraphs.zh: 漂白，用银倾煎细丝一样，只是甚热而壁乃薄，而后以，去其下面者，只留上面其薄者，中以白铜倾一无壁，以前上面安于其上，下面用银箔合其下，用焊焊之。后用滓槌槌其脚，为风锅无二。虽以凿凿开，必不能辨。如辨此，则当时烧焊之际，以火烧去其青青自然之色，如死鱼之白，故曰漂白。以此辨之，灼然明白矣。
paragraphs.en: Bleached (piaobai): silver is poured and refined just like fine-thread, only it is very hot and the walls are thin. Then the underside is taken away, leaving only the thin top. White copper is poured in the middle with no wall of its own; the former top is set on it, silver foil is joined underneath, and it is soldered. Then a dross-hammer is used on the feet, no different from a wind-pot. Even if you chisel it open you still may not tell. To identify it: at the time of soldering, fire burns away the natural bluish color, leaving a dead-fish white; hence “bleached.” Tell it this way, and it is perfectly clear.

paragraphs.zh: 煎饼银法，每铅一钱，销铜一分。若九成银一两，可用铅一两；八成可用铅二两，七成可用铅三两，灰堤中用炭装炉，慢扇其火，煎至铅化。若过后，必急扇其火，待油珠大如豆者，即以盖盖之，煞出止九五色。如待金花灿烂，煞出即结布于上，曰布心饼，又曰焦心饼。下面蟹眼回珠，二面皆白，即松纹足色。
paragraphs.en: Method for refined-cake silver: for every qian of lead, melt one fen of copper. For one tael of nine-tenths silver you may use one tael of lead; eight-tenths may use two taels of lead; seven-tenths may use three taels. In an ash dike, load charcoal in the furnace, fan the fire slowly, and refine until the lead melts. After that you must fan hard. When the oil beads are as large as beans, cover it. If you take it out then, it stops at nine-and-a-half color. If you wait until golden flowers blaze, then take it out, a crust forms on top, called cloth-heart cake, also scorched-heart cake. Below, crab-eye returning pearls; both faces white: that is pine-grain full color.

paragraphs.zh: 九成饼，亦出炉白。上乃鸡爪面，下面脚亦白。
paragraphs.en: Nine-tenths cake also comes from the furnace white. The top is a chicken-claw face; the feet below are also white.

paragraphs.zh: 八成饼，出炉略黑，必用天砂擦之方白。上面蚤斑之痕，剪开略白。
paragraphs.en: Eight-tenths cake comes from the furnace a little black; you must rub it with heaven-sand before it is white. There are flea-spot marks on top; when you snip it open it is a little white.

paragraphs.zh: 七成饼，出炉墨黑，亦用砂擦及用盐梅洗之方白，其剪口带赤。
paragraphs.en: Seven-tenths cake comes from the furnace ink-black; you also rub it with sand and wash it with salted plums before it is white; the snipped mouth has a reddish tinge.

paragraphs.zh: 六成比七成犹不同些。
paragraphs.en: Six-tenths differs a little further from seven-tenths.

paragraphs.zh: 五成即梅白饼。
paragraphs.en: Five-tenths is the plum-white cake.

paragraphs.zh: 盐烧饼，二钱五分银出一两，取出以盐烂水，调上一重在其饼上，入火烧之，取出以锤打去一重铜皮；又用盐烧之，再锤打。如此者数次，则外面铜去而自然白，曰盐烧。
paragraphs.en: Salt-burned cake: two qian five fen of silver yields one tael. Take it out, mix rotten salt water, spread a layer on the cake, put it in the fire, take it out, and hammer off a layer of copper skin; salt-burn again, hammer again. Several times like this, and the outer copper goes and it turns white of itself; this is called salt-burn.

paragraphs.zh: 白铜倾者即白盐烧。
paragraphs.en: What is poured from white copper is white salt-burn.

paragraphs.zh: 三铗饼，底是足色饼，用如纸薄，中用白饼熔一饼于中。上面用银入炉中倾出细丝，入铅二三钱，取出，泻入炭锅，成一饼样，亦用甚薄，盖于其上。然后用焊焊成一饼，铗去其四旁者，中间的饼对面剪铗，尽可瞒人。辨之其饼厚，上下皆真银，中间色目异样。知者以银面于杉木擦之，即见三样色。
paragraphs.en: Three-clip cake: the bottom is a full-color cake, thin as paper; in the middle a white cake is melted in; on top, silver is put in the furnace, poured as fine-thread, two or three qian of lead added, taken out, poured into a charcoal pan into cake shape, also very thin, and laid over the top. Then it is soldered into one cake. The four sides are clipped away; if you snip and clip the middle cake face to face, it can quite take people in. To tell it: the cake is thick; top and bottom are true silver, the middle a different color. Those who know rub the silver face on fir wood, and three colors appear at once.

paragraphs.zh: 车壳即灌铅，以松纹细丝面，以落锥落一孔，然后以割仔入其内割之，尽取其囊中者，留其银壳。后用铅灌其内填满，再用银打一尖仔尖之，又以铁錾仔錾之，如风锅一般。然辨此银，要看其两面之痕处，即见明白。
paragraphs.en: Turned-shell (cheke) is lead-filled. On a pine-grain fine-thread face, a dropping-awl makes a hole; then a cutter is put in and the inside is cut away, emptying the pouch and leaving the silver shell. Lead is then poured in to fill it; a silver point is beaten and plugged in; an iron chisel works it over, like a wind-pot. To tell this silver, look at the marks on both faces, and it is clear.

paragraphs.zh: 倒茅饼，先以上号白信石，用熔成罐不洧水者，以盐泥固济，入信石于内。打二炷香升灯盏上，轻清者听用。以银七钱、铜三钱五分熔。将起炉时，以前信石七分入银内，将盖盖之。取出天砂擦之，其面上亦鸡爪面，如九成银一般。辨之九成出炉自白，不待砂擦；然此饼铗口带黄，九成饼铗口自白。以此辨之朗然。
paragraphs.en: Inverted-thatch cake (daomao): first take top-grade white arsenolite, melt it in a jar that will not take water, seal with salt mud, put the arsenolite inside. Burn two sticks of incense under a lamp-dish; keep the light, clear part for use. Melt seven qian of silver and three qian five fen of copper. As you are about to take it from the furnace, put seven fen of the former arsenolite into the silver and cover it. Take it out and rub with heaven-sand; the face also has chicken-claw marks, like nine-tenths silver. To tell it: nine-tenths comes from the furnace white of itself and needs no sand-rubbing; but this cake’s clipped mouth has a yellow tinge, while a nine-tenths cake’s clipped mouth is white of itself. Tell it this way and it is plain.

paragraphs.zh: 更有铁线饼、江山白、华光桥、神仙饼、糁铜饼、倒插铅，其餘奇巧假银数十样，非言语笔舌所能形容。知者引申触类，观此思过半矣。有等游惰好闲、不务生理、受磨丧心、用此假银苟计衣食，以度时光，此犹穷徒，故不足责；然今贪黜之辈，家颇殷足，尚换此银，用以毒众，自图富厚，以遗子孙。不知丧心悖理，岂有善报，子孙其能昌乎！凡四民交易，止可用七成以至细丝，更低者不可用也。如昧心欺人，不唯阴遣之罪难偿，而阳报之网亦不漏矣。
paragraphs.en: There are also iron-wire cake, Jiangshan white, Huaguang Bridge, immortal cake, sprinkled-copper cake, inverted-inserted lead, and several dozen other ingenious fakes that speech and brush cannot describe. Those who know can extend the class from the instance; look at this and you have more than half. There are idlers who will not work at a living, who grind themselves down and lose all conscience, and use this fake silver as a makeshift for clothes and food to pass the time—poor wretches, not worth blaming. But now greedy, debased men, whose houses are already fairly well off, still swap this silver to poison the many, seeking wealth for themselves to leave to sons and grandsons. They do not know that those who lose conscience and go against principle have no good recompense; can their descendants flourish? In all dealings among the four classes of people, use only from seven-tenths up to fine-thread; anything lower must not be used. If you darken your heart to cheat others, not only is the unseen punishment hard to pay, the net of visible retribution will not miss you either.
